title: Seller-Brain Capture and Margin Leak Audit
one_liner: In the 90-day handover, reverse-engineer the retiring owner's pricing and rules of thumb from years of quotes and invoices, and find the contract and price leaks the seller never fixed, for a fee tied to recovered margin.
customer: First-time acquirers (search funders, independent sponsors, SBA-financed buyers, small holdcos) of $1-15M revenue service and light-manufacturing firms. SBA lenders and brokers are secondary referrers.
problem: The seller's pricing logic lives in his head, records are paper or Excel, and the handover is a 'handshake and good luck'. New owners find contractual minimums unbilled, price books frozen for years, parts sold below cost, and waste in telecom and software. They discover this only after closing, when the seller is already leaving.
solution: A 30-day sprint at signing or close. (1) Ingest 3 years of quotes, invoices, price books, contracts and vendor, phone and SaaS bills, including scanned paper. (2) An AI model reconstructs the implicit pricing rules and flags exceptions. (3) A structured, recorded 3-hour seller interview validates and labels the rules. (4) Output a working quote calculator, a written 'rules of thumb' manual, and a ranked leak list in dollars (unbilled contractual minimums, stale prices vs inflation, below-cost jobs and parts, dead subscriptions). The seller reviews the model weekly during the transition period.
why_now: Bain's 2026 reports say deals now need 10-12% EBITDA growth to hit returns and 79% of GPs expect flat purchase multiples, so operational upside has to be found rather than bought. Buyers of small firms feel the same pressure. LLMs now read messy PDFs, scans and Excel cheaply, which makes a 10-day audit cost a few hundred dollars in compute instead of a consultant's month.
revenue_model: $4-6K fixed fee for the capture sprint, plus 10-15% of annualized recovered margin in year one (capped). Optional pre-LOI 'upside memo' at $1.5-2.5K that buyers use to justify a bid and negotiate price.
non_obvious_insight: The leaks are contractual and forgotten, not strategic, and the seller's pricing logic is a perishable asset that expires with the transition period. Concrete cases from ETA operators: Tew & Taylor's contracts specified a two-hour minimum but the prior owner billed one hour, and after the buyer applied the contract rate there was 'virtually no customer pushback' (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). At Cardinal Heating & Air, prices were unchanged since pre-COVID, parts were sold below cost, and the buyer cut $1.4M of annualized cost in two weeks ($10K/month in cell phones vs $3K needed). Gross margins went from 7-20% to 48-49% (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/mike-bourgeois-cardinal-heating-and-air). At Winsor Fireform, pricing was the seller's 27 years of 'hunches', and the buyers 'sprinted' to extract it into a model during his 3-month transition; gross margin rose from 55% to 58-59% (https://acquiringminds.co/articles/andrew-sova-alex-clark-winsor-fireform-novo-foundry). At Gary Air, prices had not kept pace with inflation for 4+ years, and earnings went from $340K SDE to $1.3M EBITDA in 14 months (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/rob-brooks-gary-air). Four independent buyers found the same class of leak and each rebuilt it by hand.
first_30_days: Offer free audits to 10 first-time buyers found in ETA communities (Searchfunder, Acquiring Minds audience, ETA subreddits) in exchange for permission to publish anonymized before/after numbers. Build parsers for QuickBooks exports and for invoice exports from ServiceTitan, Jobber and Housecall Pro, plus a vendor-bill classifier. Create a one-page seller-interview protocol. Convert the first 3 free audits into case studies, then switch to contingency pricing.

title: Revenue Recovery From Blocked Shopping Agents
one_liner: Synthetic agent shoppers try to buy from your store every night, find where bot defenses and checkout kill legitimate agent orders, and you pay a cut of the sales recovered.
customer: Mid-market e-commerce merchants ($5M-$200M GMV) on Shopify Plus, BigCommerce or Adobe Commerce with aggressive bot, WAF and fraud settings, reached through their agencies and fraud vendors.
problem: Insiders think the bottleneck is protocol adoption (ACP vs UCP vs AP2). The measurable leak is simpler. Agent usage is about 62% at comparison but only about 23% at checkout. Fraud and bot systems built for humans misclassify agent traffic (Chargebacks911 warns of a false-decline problem). CAPTCHAs, SMS one-time codes and 3DS challenges kill legitimate agent orders, and the lost sale looks like a bounce, so no dashboard shows it.
solution: Run real agent stacks (ChatGPT agent mode, Comet, Gemini, open-source browser agents, plus ACP/UCP/AP2 clients) through scripted purchase journeys on the live store with test cards. Log the exact failure point: challenge page, WAF rule, OTP step, stale feed, price mismatch. Deliver a weekly fix list (allowlist verified agent signatures, rule changes, checkout patches), then re-test to prove recovery.
why_now: Bots now outnumber humans. Stores that blocked AI bots in 2024 are undoing it, and the Ninth Circuit ruling makes user-directed agents legitimate visitors. Five competing checkout protocols make failure modes hard to see.
revenue_model: $2-5k fixed audit plus 5-10% of attributable recovered agent revenue for 12 months, or $500-$2k/month monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: A performance-fee audit is easy to buy because the merchant risks nothing. The proof is measurable (before and after test purchases), and the data becomes a benchmark of which defenses block which agents.
first_30_days: Build the harness with 3 agent stacks and 5 common checkout and WAF patterns. Offer 10 free audits to Shopify agencies who can resell. Convert the first 3 leaks worth over $5k per month into revenue-share contracts.

title: Layoff Early-Warning for Credit Unions
one_liner: Turns public WARN notices and layoff signals into member-level outreach lists, so lenders can offer hardship plans about 60 days before payments are missed.
customer: Credit unions (roughly 4,400 in the US), community banks, mortgage servicers and auto lenders pay $1.5-6k a month, often via credit-union service organisations.
problem: White-collar layoffs are lumpy and local (information-sector employment fell 23k in one Aug 2026 month, Amazon cut ~16,000 corporate roles). Lenders learn about them from missed payments, when charge-off risk is already high and members are hardest to help. Hardship programs exist but outreach comes too late.
solution: Ingest state WARN databases, news and layoff trackers. Match employers to the lender's book using payroll ACH descriptors on member accounts. Rank members by exposure, then supply compliant outreach scripts, pre-approved skip-a-pay or modification offers, and uplift measurement.
why_now: Layoffs are steady and concentrated in higher-balance, AI-exposed white-collar borrowers. Payroll descriptors and open-banking data make the join easy. Small lenders have no data teams, and the low-hire market makes re-employment slow (7-13 months in practitioner reports).
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-6k a month per institution, or a performance fee on avoided delinquencies.
non_obvious_insight: The layoffs are public. The scarce piece is the join to the lender's book via payroll descriptors. Employees of a laid-off employer often bank at the same local credit union, so the risk is concentrated, and the ROI is stated in avoided charge-offs rather than charity.
first_30_days: Normalise 50 state WARN sources. Backtest with a friendly credit union on two past layoff events to show missed payments 45-90 days later. Get two credit-union service organisations to run a paid $1k-a-month pilot.

title: Passive-Radar Drone Detection for Prisons
one_liner: Detect small drones by listening to ambient cell, broadcast and Wi-Fi signals, with no transmitter, no license and no radar permit.
customer: State departments of corrections, county jails, and secondary customers such as critical infrastructure and stadiums.
problem: Cape Canaveral radars see aircraft up to a 747 but not a quadcopter. State prisons face contraband drops with low budgets and cannot deploy active radar or jammers. Remote ID and RF detection miss drones that are not broadcasting.
solution: A rooftop kit of low-cost software-defined radios using the signal reflections of existing cell towers and broadcast transmitters, with ML-based detection of small-drone Doppler signatures. It alerts a mobile app and logs evidence for prosecution, and it is passive so legal risk is minimal.
why_now: Cheap SDRs and modern ML make passive sensing of low-cross-section targets feasible in 2025-26. Small-drone detection is now flagged as thin even at major federal sites, and drone traffic is exploding with 200,000-unit purchases (verify feasibility and prison contraband scale).
revenue_model: $25-60K per site installation plus $500-1,500 per month for software and monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Passivity is the business model. Local agencies cannot legally emit RF or mitigate, so a purely receiving sensor is the only kind they can buy without federal permission.
first_30_days: Recruit one university RF lab. Pilot on a rooftop with an existing tower nearby and log real drone passes. Approach 3 state corrections security chiefs for a paid pilot.

title: Operator-of-Record for Enterprise Drone Flights
one_liner: A licensed BVLOS operations team-as-a-service that files the waivers, runs the safety case and supervises the flights for utilities, solar developers and pipeline owners.
customer: Mid-size utilities and co-ops, solar and wind developers, pipeline and rail operators, ports, mines, and their insurers.
problem: BVLOS technology is ready, but organizations lack the capability: waiver applications, safety cases, ops manuals, remote-pilot staffing and data pipelines. The final status of Part 108 (the FAA BVLOS rule) could not be verified, which adds uncertainty. Meanwhile the DJI ban forces fleet refreshes.
solution: A reusable safety-case library and remote-pilot center (one pilot supervising 5-10 drone docks) running US-made drone-in-a-box fleets. Price per line-mile or per site, with data delivered into the customer's GIS and maintenance systems.
why_now: The December 2025 DJI restrictions force fleet replacement decisions in 2026, and Wing's 1M deliveries show BVLOS operations working at scale. Whatever Part 108's final form, operators still need documented safety cases and waivers.
revenue_model: $5-20k per month per site retainer or per-line-mile pricing on multi-year MSAs, plus waiver and safety-case consulting fees.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation is a one-time cost that vendors avoid, but the operator-of-record that accumulates waivers, flight logs and accepted safety cases builds a moat that compounds with every approval.
first_30_days: Pick one region (for example co-ops in Texas or Colorado) and partner with one US-made dock vendor. Get one co-op to sign a pilot covering 20 substations, file the waiver, and aim for the first inspection within 60 days.

title: Turn Foreman Paper Sign-In Sheets Into Court-Ready Records
one_liner: Foremen text a photo of the daily paper sign-in sheet, and the system timestamps it, flags overtime, break and travel-time errors, and builds an audit-ready record. The crew changes nothing.
customer: Trade subcontractors with 5 to 50 field employees (electrical, framing, concrete, HVAC, roofing) that still use paper sheets or Excel. It is sold through construction-focused insurance agents, payroll providers and construction CPAs.
problem: Most contractor wage-hour violations are recordkeeping failures: overtime miscalculations, uncompensated travel time and undocumented breaks. Paper sheets and foreman memory have no audit trail, so when a wage claim lands up to two years later the employer cannot prove what it paid. A $50,000 overtime dispute can double with liquidated damages before attorney fees. Owners don't buy time-tracking software for compliance, because compliance is not what they think they are buying.
solution: A phone number or WhatsApp thread. The foreman photographs the day's sign-in sheet, and the service extracts hours per worker, adds a trusted timestamp, and stores the original image in an append-only log with a chain-of-custody hash. Each week it reconciles hours against the payroll export (CSV from ADP, Gusto or QuickBooks Payroll) and flags mismatches: overtime not paid, drive time between sites, missing breaks, and prevailing-wage or certified-payroll classification gaps. When a claim or audit arrives, one click produces a records package with an affidavit-ready custodian statement. Insurance partners can offer it as a loss-control benefit on wage-and-hour or EPLI coverage.
why_now: Construction Dive ran this as a July 2026 compliance story. DOL Wage and Hour recovered more than $259 million in back wages for nearly 177,000 workers in fiscal 2025, and construction alone saw about 3,000 investigations and $36 million recovered for 21,000 workers. The labor squeeze, with job openings rising for a third month, keeps overtime and crew-hopping high. Photo capture, OCR and trusted timestamping are now cheap enough to deliver this for about $100 a month.
revenue_model: $99 to $299 per month per contractor by headcount; a $750 audit-response records package; a 15 to 20% recurring rebate to insurance agents or payroll partners who resell. Later add payroll-error recovery reports as a paid add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Apps like time clocks fail because crews resist changing habits, and buyers don't feel compliance risk. So sell defensibility on top of the existing paper behavior instead of replacing it. Evidence: a survey of 180 mid-market contractors found only 4% cited compliance as a concern with time tracking, and 72% who tracked time on paper or spreadsheets 'never raised a compliance concern once in the conversation'. The article notes the records 'can't answer the question' when disputes arise two years later, and cites $259M in DOL back wages and $36M recovered from construction in a single year (https://www.constructiondive.com/news/inaccurate-time-records-contractor-compliance-liability/825438/). The same Construction Dive labor page shows the squeeze (https://www.constructiondive.com/topic/labor/).
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit 5 contractors via a construction CPA or insurance agent friend, and build the intake as a shared phone number plus a spreadsheet and an OCR script. Weeks 2 to 3: run their real sign-in sheets through it, deliver a weekly variance report, and show each owner one specific overtime or drive-time gap. Week 4: charge $149 per month, and present the results to two construction insurance agencies as a loss-control add-on. Target: 8 paying contractors and 1 signed agency partner.

title: Orphan Appliance Parts, Crowdsourced From Repair Techs
one_liner: Quirky (dead 2015) crowdsourced gadgets from hobbyist inventors; the 2026 version prints the discontinued $6 plastic part that keeps a $900 appliance out of the landfill, and pays the repair tech who specced it a royalty.
customer: Independent appliance repair shops (about 10-20 techs per metro market) and multifamily property-maintenance teams that manage hundreds of identical fridges, washers and dishwashers; DIY owners and EU repair cafes come second via marketplace listings.
problem: A brittle plastic piece (fridge door bin, dishwasher rack wheel, washer lid-lock striker, range knob, vacuum gear) is discontinued, backordered for weeks, or OEM-priced at $50-90. Techs condemn a machine over a $6 part, and landlords swap whole units. Techs see the same failure dozens of times but have no channel to monetize that knowledge.
solution: A tech texts a photo and model number. An AI-assisted CAD step plus human check produces a measured model. The part is printed in nylon or carbon-filled PETG through Xometry/Craftcloud-type bureaus, or a small in-house farm. It gets a SKU page, a fit guarantee (free reprint if wrong) and a 10% lifetime royalty to the originating tech. Non-safety-critical parts only: no heating elements, gas, or oven door latches. Shops pay $29/mo for a private request queue, 48-hour dispatch and a discount. Property managers get bulk catalogs per building.
why_now: The EU Right to Repair Directive's national transposition deadline passed on 31 July 2026. It requires spare parts at reasonable prices and bars manufacturers from blocking independent repairers who use compatible or 3D-printed parts. Several US states (CA, NY, MN, OR) have repair laws. Photo-to-CAD tools are good enough and print-on-demand bureaus are cheap. Tariffs have pushed new-appliance prices up, so repair economics are better than in 2015.
revenue_model: Part sales at $18-35 (roughly 50-65% gross margin after print and shipping); $29/mo shop membership; annual bulk contracts with property managers; royalty payouts as the growth loop. Later, license CAD to mid-size OEMs that need cheap R2R-compliant spares for out-of-production models.
non_obvious_insight: Quirky's crowd was the wrong crowd: hobbyist inventors with no ground truth about what breaks. The right crowd already exists in the field: techs who see failure modes daily and lack a way to get paid for that. The right buyer is not the DIYer but a pro or landlord for whom a $12 part avoids a $900 replacement. The orphan-part long tail is what 3D printing is naturally good at, and the R2R text neutralizes OEM opposition.
first_30_days: Pick fridges and dishwashers from 2005-2015. Mine r/appliancerepair, eBay sold listings and out-of-stock parts pages for the 25 most-failed brittle plastics. Model and print them via two bureaus and list on eBay, Etsy and Shopify with the fit guarantee. Recruit 15 local techs from Facebook groups with the royalty offer, and pilot with 3 property managers. Under $10k of spend; target 150 orders.

title: Walker Brain: Clip-On Sensor for Rollators
one_liner: A $60 clip-on pod that turns any walker or rollator into a fall alarm, night-light and gait-speed monitor, so there is no wearable to forget.
customer: Home-care agencies and PACE programs (buying for clients), DME suppliers, Medicare Advantage and ACO care teams, and adult children buying directly.
problem: Pendant alarms fail because many seniors won't wear them or press them. People who use walkers are among the highest fall-risk group, yet smart-walker work is mostly academic prototypes. Gait speed predicts decline and hospitalization but is measured in a clinic once a year, if at all.
solution: A clamp-on pod with an IMU, LTE-M connectivity, a small LED light strip, tip and fall detection and grip sensing. It detects when the walker is actually being used versus left by the bed at night, which is itself a leading risk signal. It auto-alerts on tipping and sends a weekly gait report and decline flags to family and the care team. Battery lasts months and the senior needs no app.
why_now: Low-power LTE-M and IMU chips are cheap. Medicare Advantage plans are measured on fall-risk management, and home-care agencies are looking for differentiation. The DME channel has not changed in decades, and the walker sensor category is still mostly prototypes.
revenue_model: Hardware $59-79, family subscription $8-12/month. B2B: about $6 per pod per month for agencies, or a per-member-per-month fee for plan pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Don't ask an 80-year-old to adopt a new device. Instrument the one object they can't give up and that is with them exactly when risk peaks. 'Walker left behind at night' is a signal no wearable can capture.
first_30_days: Prototype with off-the-shelf LTE-M dev boards and a 3D-printed clamp. Place 30 pods on walkers with 3 home-care agencies as free trials. Measure alerts and gait trends. Aim to convert 2 agencies to 100-unit pilots, and talk to outpatient physical therapists about a small validation study.

title: Royalty Co-op for Expert Robot Demonstrations
one_liner: A worker-owned data cooperative where master tradespeople record their skilled work and earn ongoing royalties when robot makers license the demonstrations.
customer: Payers are robot foundation-model teams and manipulation or humanoid startups that buy data. Suppliers are skilled tradespeople such as tire techs, electricians, welders and HVAC technicians.
problem: Data platforms pay flat hourly rates for average people making coffee. Robots need expert-quality demonstrations, and experts will not sell their edge for a one-time $20 an hour or train their own replacement without control and upside.
solution: Partner with a union local or trade school. Members use standardized capture kits (head and wrist cameras, gloves) with quality scoring. They get a guaranteed hourly rate, 30-50% of licensing revenue, and a veto over use cases. Buyers pay per curated dataset plus a royalty per training run.
why_now: Robot training data is the humanoid bottleneck. XDOF reached about $50M annualized revenue within three months of stealth, and Mecka projects $100M ARR by end-2026 on a roughly $500M valuation. Willingness to pay is proven, while worker anxiety about being trained out of a job is rising.
revenue_model: $50-500k per dataset license, with a 20-30% cooperative fee on royalties and licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Data quality follows expert willingness, and willingness follows ownership. A cooperative with collective pricing power is a supply moat that flat-wage crowd platforms cannot copy, and it turns worker fear into the product's selling point.
first_30_days: Partner with one trade school and one union local in tire and auto service or EV-charger installation. Recruit 20 masters and capture 200 hours of one task family. Sell a pilot dataset to 2 robotics startups at $30-80k.

title: Bonded US-Only Remote Operators for Robots
one_liner: A staffing company for physical AI: background-checked, bonded, US-resident remote operators working from secure facilities on SLA-backed shifts to assist robotaxis, delivery robots and teleoperated humanoids.
customer: AV fleets, sidewalk and delivery robot operators, humanoid and mobile-manipulation startups (Series A to C) and the enterprise or health customers who demand US-based, vetted humans. The buyer is the head of operations or safety.
problem: Autonomy plateaus at 99%, and the last 1% is human labor. Waymo disclosed at a February 2026 Senate hearing that some remote assistance staff are in the Philippines, drawing political heat (Sen. Markey called it a safety issue). 1X's Neo puts a remote operator with a VR headset inside customers' homes, which is the central privacy objection. Robot startups have no staffing operation for 24/7 shift coverage, vetting, training, security controls and quality scoring.
solution: Secure operator centers (not homes) staffed with vetted US-resident operators drawn from gamers, drone pilots, veterans and military spouses. Certification per partner interface, quality scoring, audit trails and a 'named operator and session log' feature so a homeowner or hospital can see who touched what. Start with teleoperation for data collection and pilot demos, then move into live remote assistance and compliance packs.
why_now: Consumer humanoids and expanding robotaxi fleets (Waymo alone is at about 500k paid rides a week across 14 cities) make operator-hours a rapidly scaling cost. The Senate scrutiny of offshore remote assistance and the Neo privacy debate mean a 'US-only, vetted, auditable' premium is about to be demanded by regulators and enterprise buyers.
revenue_model: Billed operator-hours at $40-70/hour against a loaded cost of $25-30/hour. Premiums for compliance, security clearance and named-operator features. Setup fees for integration and certification.
non_obvious_insight: Every 10,000 robots create thousands of operator jobs, and the political fight will be about where those people sit, just as with call centers. Whoever builds the trusted, audited labor pool early owns a compliance premium that AI labs cannot easily build in-house.
first_30_days: Rent a 10-seat secured room in a mid-cost city. Buy Quest headsets and a leader-follower arm set. Recruit 15 operators from gaming and RC-drone communities and pass them through background checks. Offer 100 pilot-hours at cost-plus to 10 humanoid and delivery-robot startups who need demo and data collection help.

title: GPS Spoofing Alarm Using LEO Signals
one_liner: A passive receiver that listens to Starlink, OneWeb and Iridium-style signals and flags when GPS disagrees.
customer: Shipping companies and port authorities in jammed regions (Baltic, Persian Gulf, Red Sea), aviation operators, telecom timing operators, drone fleets, and hull and P&I insurers.
problem: GNSS jamming and spoofing have spread across shipping and aviation (prior knowledge, 2024-25). Most detection depends on GNSS itself or expensive inertial systems. Operators and insurers want independent evidence of position integrity.
solution: A small software-defined receiver that measures Doppler and timing from LEO communication signals of opportunity and, using public orbit data, checks position and time consistency. First product is an integrity alarm, not a navigator. Later add tens-of-meters holdover navigation.
why_now: There are about 10,000 Starlinks plus other constellations, so signals of opportunity are abundant. Academic demonstrations of positioning from them have matured. Jamming has moved from a defense concern to a commercial one.
revenue_model: $2-5k per unit plus $100 per month cloud analytics. Insurer-funded fleet programs. Government pilots.
non_obvious_insight: You do not need to navigate better than GPS to be valuable, only to disagree with it reliably. Integrity is a cheaper, faster product than replacement navigation.
first_30_days: Build a lab proof of concept using a Ku-band LNB and an SDR. Recruit two Baltic or Gulf ship managers or port operators for field trials. Approach one marine insurer about premium credits for verified integrity.

title: Hazmat Sidecar for Small Old-House Repairs
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing shortage/trades labor/home services x Waste/recycling/circular economy/critical minerals/materials
one_liner: A flat-price, same-week asbestos and lead test-and-remove service that solo-to-five-tech plumbing, HVAC, electrical and flooring shops call when a small job in a pre-1980 house hits suspect material, with the waste manifest handled for them.
customer: Small trade shops (pay per call and pass through) and homeowners; property managers are a later segment.
problem: Median home age is 44 years and 62% of homeowners now choose repair over replace, so small jobs constantly disturb duct wrap, vinyl tile, transite, plaster and lead paint. Licensed abatement firms impose $2-5K minimums and weeks of lead time, so contractors either walk away (feeding the 73% project backlog) or cut corners and carry liability. Few landfills accept asbestos waste, and manifests and pre-notification confuse small shops.
solution: A van with two accredited techs: same-week sample results through a partner lab, flat-fee minor removal where state rules allow (subcontracted where they don't), bagged, labeled and manifested disposal, and a digital clearance letter the trade can hand the homeowner. Shops book by text and can subscribe for priority.
why_now: Repair-over-replace, tariff-inflated equipment and HVAC's 2025 shipment trough leave small shops chasing any billable job and unwilling to lose one to a hazmat surprise. Larger platforms (ServiceTitan, PE roll-ups) do not serve sub-$10K jobs.
revenue_model: $300-1,500 per job; per-sample testing fees; $99/mo priority subscription for trade shops.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not removal labor but the disposal chain: manifests, landfill acceptance and pollution insurance. Owning that chain lets one small team become the referral default for every trade in the area.
first_30_days: Days 1-30: complete state inspector accreditation, lead-safe firm certification and worker courses, get a pollution-liability quote and sign a landfill acceptance agreement. Meanwhile pre-sign 10 trade shops to a flat-price menu. Days 30-90: run the first 20 jobs and refine pricing.

title: Childcare Credits Instead of Builder Rate Buydowns
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing/skilled-trades/home services x Parenting/childcare deserts/Gen Alpha/kids and AI-screens
one_liner: Homebuilders replace temporary mortgage rate buydowns with redeemable childcare credits, and the program builds the licensed care space inside the community.
customer: Small and mid-size spec and production builders with unsold inventory in family-heavy exurbs (Sunbelt and Midwest), and master-planned community developers. The end buyers are young families with kids under 5.
problem: 63% of builders use incentives and 80-90% of new-home sales need rate buydowns with 30-year rates near 7%, yet completions fell 27.1% year over year. Buydowns are a one-time cost that fades in 2-3 years. For a household with toddlers, childcare ($13,128 per child, more than a mortgage for two kids in 45 states) is the actual affordability wall, and new suburbs are childcare deserts.
solution: The builder funds a Family Care Credit (for example $400 a month for 24 months) redeemable only at licensed providers in a vetted network. The startup pre-commits reserved occupancy with providers and helps a provider open in the community, using a builder-built care-ready clubhouse room, flex unit or model home at cost. The credit's cost accrues only when used, so expected builder spend can undercut a $12-20K buydown. Marketing kit: 'move-in ready, childcare included'.
why_now: Incentives are at a cyclical high, starts are steady but completions fell 27.1% and builders are financing shops. ROAD to Housing Act streamlining for small multifamily and factory-built homes aims at exactly these family starter products. Dependent-care FSA limits rose to $7,500, and childcare deserts are politically salient.
revenue_model: 10-15% program fee on credit dollars funded by the builder, per-family placement fee from providers, and later a margin on prepaid-slot financing.
non_obvious_insight: Builders see incentives as price cuts, but a family with a toddler values $400 a month of childcare more than a temporary rate cut. A builder is already a construction company, so converting a room to licensed space costs them little and is worth a rent-free facility to a provider. The guaranteed occupancy is what makes the provider's economics work in the first place.
first_30_days: Target five small builders with spec inventory in fast-growing exurbs. Check local childcare deserts with the CAP map, sign one builder for a 10-home pilot, and line up two licensed home providers. Launch a 'move-in ready with childcare' landing page and compare lead conversion to the builder's buydown ads. Have counsel confirm the credit's treatment against buyer-concession rules.

title: Ulysses Contracts for AI Use in Psychosis Recovery
one_liner: A patient-signed pre-commitment plus an app that adds friction and alerts a trusted contact when a recovering patient's chatbot use starts to spiral.
customer: Early-psychosis and community mental-health programs ($15-30 per patient per month) and families of people with a prior psychotic or manic episode ($12 a month).
problem: Trend chain: chatbot sycophancy leads to documented chatbot-linked psychosis (UCSF's Keith Sakata treated 12 cases; the Human Line Project spans 22 countries), then people with prior episodes are the most exposed, then clinicians can only say 'avoid chatbots' and families cannot police 3 a.m. sessions. Psychiatric advance directives cover hospitalization, not AI use.
solution: (1) A one-page 'AI Use Advance Directive' completed with the treating clinician while the patient is well. (2) A device-level app that watches patterns locally (late-night sessions, session length and, with consent, on-device classification of grandiose or mission-style themes) and applies escalating friction: delay, grounding script, message to a trusted contact, weekly clinician summary. (3) Data stays on the device except the escalation flag.
why_now: OpenAI's own Oct 2025 estimate (0.07% of weekly users show signs of psychosis or mania) implies hundreds of thousands of people. Regulation is bans and disclosures, not protection at the device level. On-device small models now make private classification feasible, and no lab has to cooperate.
revenue_model: Per-patient monthly licenses to programs (early-psychosis programs have dedicated public funding) and a $12 monthly family plan. Later: payer and long-acting-injectable partner programs.
non_obvious_insight: The winning product is not a smarter chatbot but a pre-commitment device, the same logic as psychiatric advance directives: the well self binds the unwell self. Because it lives at the device layer, it works across every model.
first_30_days: Recruit two early-psychosis programs via clinician advisors. Draft the directive template with them. Build an Android-first usage monitor (fastest to ship) and test it with about 15 patients. Sell programs a $5k pilot.

title: Health-Check Weekends Abroad, Vetted by US Doctors
one_liner: Three- to four-day trips to Korean and Japanese comprehensive screening centers, with a US physician who prepares you before, translates results after, and coordinates follow-up back home.
customer: Americans 45-65 who pay cash for screening: self-employed, pre-Medicare early retirees, high-deductible households. The wedge is Korean-American and Japanese-American families who already fly to visit parents and trust the hospitals; the broader market follows.
problem: US preventive imaging and endoscopy are sold a la carte and priced for insurers: one whole-body MRI can cost $2,500, and an MRI plus CT plus endoscopy plus cardiac workup can run to several thousand dollars out of pocket. Korea and Japan built prevention into national habit, with one-day comprehensive packages (imaging, endoscopy, cardiac, labs) that reportedly cost 40-70% less than equivalent US screening, but US patients cannot navigate the language, the choice of package or the follow-up when they return.
solution: A packaged trip: (1) pre-trip telehealth visit with a US physician who picks an evidence-based subset of tests and avoids overkill; (2) land package with hotel, interpreter and escort at a vetted university hospital health-promotion center, results in days; (3) post-trip visit where the physician turns the translated report into a US action plan and books any follow-up at home. Group departures create cohorts and lower unit costs. Pair with the Workup Cover idea for the tail if a finding appears.
why_now: Consumers have shown in 2025-26 that they will pay $800-$2,500 cash for a single scan, and K-culture has made Korea an aspirational destination for Americans. Korean hospitals run international patient centers and take intermediary partners, and international screening packages are now marketed in English. US screening costs, high deductibles and the coming FDA and Medicare changes for blood-based tests are widening the gap.
revenue_model: Package margin of 15-25% (travel margin plus hospital partner commission where legal), $250 per physician consult (pre and post), and group or employer retreat pricing for early-retiree communities and small businesses. Optional membership for annual return trips.
non_obvious_insight: The right pitch is not 'cheap surgery abroad', which has a bad reputation, but 'join a country where prevention is a national habit'. The unclaimed value is not the discount but de-risking the two ends of the trip: choosing tests that matter and handling the follow-up in the US. The diaspora is the natural wedge because trust, language and family visits already exist.
first_30_days: Contact the international health-screening centers of three Seoul hospitals and agree one standard package and one heart-focused package. Recruit a telehealth-licensed US physician for pre- and post-trip visits. Recruit 20 pilot travelers from Korean-American church and community groups and longevity forums, take $500 deposits for a first group departure four to five months out, and get six seats confirmed. Keep marketing to screening and prevention, not diagnosis or cure.

title: Blank-and-Recipe Kits for Desktop UV Printer Owners
one_liner: A monthly kit of pre-cut blanks, matched jigs and pre-calibrated height maps for the roughly 23,000 desktop UV printers that crowdfunding put into homes, so owners can fill machines and sell without fixturing trial-and-error.
customer: Owners of eufyMake E1, Longer ePrint and HeyGears-class desktop UV printers: Etsy and craft-fair sellers, keycap and phone-case micro-brands, makerspaces. Payer is the printer owner running a side business.
problem: Owners paid $1,500-$2,700 for a machine but still need to source consistent blanks, build registration jigs, tune 2.5D height maps, and finish for durability. Files are sold ad hoc on Etsy, but the hard part is physical fixturing and repeatability, so machines sit idle.
solution: A subscription that ships 30-50 laser-cut or CNC blanks (acrylic coasters, aluminium tags, keycaps, phone-case shells), a laser-cut alignment jig sized to the printer's bed, and a bundled PNG plus height map plus 'recipe card' (curing, primer and clear-coat steps) tested on the E1 and Longer. Add wholesale blank packs for sellers who want to scale, plus a 'sell this next' trend drop based on Etsy search data.
why_now: eufyMake E1 became Kickstarter's most funded project ever ($46.76M, 17,822 backers), Longer added $4.2M (1,584 backers) and HeyGears G1 $17.4M (3,911 backers). Units delivered from late 2025 through 2026 mean roughly 23,000 new owners are hitting the practical limits of the hobby now, and Etsy already has listings for E1 jigs and height-map bundles.
revenue_model: $59/mo blank-and-recipe kit, $0.40-$1.20 per blank wholesale packs (55-65% gross margin), and $19 add-on jig files. Later, sell a validated-blank certification to printer makers.
non_obvious_insight: Files are already a commodity on Etsy (e.g. 'Full Honor Set' bundles with PNG, Height Map, Print Guide, and popular E1 jigs, https://www.etsy.com/market/uv_printer_file), and the printer makers fight over ink instead. Owners' real pain is physical: one review notes prints need protective finishing, flat prints take minutes but textured pieces close to an hour, and heavy users hit ink-expiry chips (about GBP 240 of dead ink after seven months, https://www.makerhacks.com/eufymake-e1-review/), which a GitHub project was created to work around (https://github.com/joggie/eufy-timewarp). The same review says the business is 'high margin, low volume' (a keychain costing 85p sells for GBP 10-15; a GBP 5-8 tumbler up to GBP 25). Sellers who scale need repeatable blanks and jigs more than another file, and a consumable-with-recipe product is sold to them, not to the vendor. Demand sizing: https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/3d-printer-breaks-kickstarter-record-raises-44m/493857 and https://www.gizmocrowd.com/top-crowdfunding-campaigns.
first_30_days: Buy one E1-class printer (or borrow from an owner) and produce 3 kit designs: acrylic keychain, aluminium tag, keycap. Sell 50 founding kits at $49 in the eufyMake users Facebook group and r/UVprinting. Share before/after photos and per-piece margin math. Use a local laser-cut shop for blanks and collect feedback to lock registration tolerances.

title: Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers
one_liner: A verified job-placement and completion ledger that makes short-term training programs (CDL, CNA, welding, HVAC, medical assistant, cosmetology) audit-ready for the governor and Secretary approvals that Workforce Pell requires.
customer: Small proprietary career schools, community college workforce and continuing-education units, and employer-training nonprofits running 8-15 week programs. The program owner or director pays. State workforce boards are a second buyer because they were given no new resources to verify placement.
problem: The Workforce Pell final rule (published May 19, 2026; effective July 20, 2026, with early implementation from July 1) covers programs of 150-599 clock hours and 8-15 weeks. A program must show 70% completion and 70% job placement, measured over the 12 months before it applies and annually after that. The governor must first certify the program as high-skill, high-wage or in-demand, then the Secretary approves. Providers must submit completer lists and the information needed to verify placement. Commenters flagged burden for small providers and noted states got no new resources to run the framework. Separately, the earnings-premium rule (effective July 1, 2027) strips Direct Loan access from programs that fail in two of three consecutive years. The Department estimated 93% of cosmetology programs would fail under the proposal.
solution: At completion the system automatically sends completers and employers text and email verification requests at 30, 90 and 180 days. It collects pay stubs, employer confirmations and consent for state wage-record matching, and reconciles them to the rule's placement definition. It produces the governor's application packet (completer list, placement evidence, tuition versus earnings benchmarks) and the annual recertification. It also scores each existing program's exposure to the earnings-premium test using public program-level earnings data so owners can decide what to keep, fix or convert into a short-term program.
why_now: The 12-month look-back means a provider that is not tracking verified placement now cannot apply in 2027. The earnings-premium test takes effect July 1, 2027 and is already being scored on 2021 completers' 2025 earnings. States are building governor-approval processes this fall, and Workforce Pell went live July 2026.
revenue_model: $4-12k per year per program subscription, or $150-300 per completer verified. $3-5k fixed fee for the governor application packet. Earnings-premium exposure report for $1.5-3k. Later, licensing to state workforce boards for verification.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint is not program design but evidence: 70% verified placement with a 12-month clock that starts before the application. Short-course providers such as CDL, CNA and barbering schools typically track completion, not verified employment, so most will discover the gap after the clock has started. The final rule requires providers to give the Governor 'necessary information to verify the job placement rate', and it aggregates small programs' completers up to four award years to reach a 30-student minimum, which favors providers with clean historical records. The Title IV survival angle (93% of cosmetology programs were projected to fail the earnings test under the proposal) gives the same customer a second, more urgent reason to buy. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/19/2026-10013/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand-driven-workforce-pell-pell-grant and https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/01/2026-13286/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand--driven-workforce-pell-student-tuition
first_30_days: Pick two states whose governors have opened a Workforce Pell approval process. Recruit five schools in different fields, including one at-risk cosmetology school, with a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text and employer email to produce a baseline verified placement rate. Deliver a sample governor packet and an earnings-premium exposure score for each. Use the results to pitch the state workforce board on verification capacity.

title: Smell Graders for Recycled Plastic
one_liner: A network of trained human noses that gives every batch of post-consumer recycled plastic an odor grade from 1 to 5, creating the price tier and spec that brands need to hit recycled-content mandates.
customer: Plastic recyclers selling PCR resin (HDPE, PP), converters that mold bottles and tubs, and brand owners in personal care, household and food buying PCR under EU and US recycled-content rules. The recyclers' quality managers buy first, then brand procurement teams.
problem: Odor is one of the biggest barriers to using recycled plastic. Recyclers can't tell buyers reliably what a batch smells like. Brands reject loads or cap PCR percentages out of caution. Lab methods such as GC-olfactometry are slow and costly, and there's no shared odor grade the way coffee has the Q-score.
solution: A standard protocol (heated headspace jars, blind triplicates, a reference odor kit, descriptor vocabulary such as rancid, detergent, smoky) run by a panel of trained sniffers recruited from perfumers, coffee Q-graders, sommeliers and food-sensory panelists. Recyclers mail samples and get a 48-hour graded report. Human scores then train an e-nose and GC model that lowers cost per test. Over time it becomes a certification: license and train graders, and publish the grade spec brands cite in purchase contracts.
why_now: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation applies from 12 August 2026, with 2030 recycled-content minimums (30% for contact-sensitive PET, 10% for other contact-sensitive plastics). Brands have to buy far more PCR within a few years. Sensor vendors need human-panel labels to train on, and none has a standard odor tier to price against.
revenue_model: $120 to $250 per batch grade. Weekly-lot subscriptions for recyclers. Vendor-qualification programs for brands at $30k or more per year. Grader certification and training fees. Licensing of the labeled dataset to e-nose makers.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation mandates recycled content, but a human nose decides whether the resin is usable, and buyers will not trust a grade until someone standardizes it. Whoever owns the grading standard sets the price tiers for the whole PCR market, a bit like coffee's Q-grading. Human panels remain the legal and commercial ground truth even after e-noses arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 sniffers from local specialty roasters and perfume or flavor schools. Buy vials, a hot plate and a reference odor kit for under $1,000. Offer three regional recyclers free grading of 20 batches each, and check the grades against their buyers' rejection history. Then price it. Publish a free 'PCR smell atlas' to attract recycler and brand inbound.

title: Outsourced Elder-Exploitation Desk for Credit Unions
one_liner: A managed service where trained specialists take flagged older-member transactions, call the member and trusted contact, file reports and document compliance.
customer: Community banks and credit unions ($300M-$5B in assets) with older memberships. Sales run through CUSOs, state leagues and core-processor marketplaces to BSA and fraud officers.
problem: Americans 60+ reported $7.7B in fraud losses in 2025 (up 59%), with an average loss over $38k and 12,400+ people losing $100k or more. Small institutions have alerts but no trained humans to call members, coordinate lawful holds, file SARs and APS reports, and prove Senior Safe Act training.
solution: Ingest the institution's flagged-alert queue and staff a desk with retired bank fraud investigators and social workers who use scripts to break the scam spell (pig-butchering, crypto-ATM, impostor). The desk coordinates holds, files APS and SAR narratives, runs annual Senior Safe Act training, and delivers quarterly avoided-loss analytics.
why_now: Investment and pig-butchering fraud is over a third of losses, older adults are adopting AI fast (23% of 65+ use ChatGPT, up from 10%), and voice-cloning scams raise stakes. State attorneys general and regulators are pressing institutions to do more.
revenue_model: $2-6k a month per institution by asset size, plus per-case fees, sold on documented avoided loss.
non_obvious_insight: Consumer fraud apps are crowded, but the institution is the party with a duty of care, and the missing capacity is human case handling, not another detection model. Pricing to avoided losses makes the ROI obvious.
first_30_days: Sell a 90-day pilot to two credit unions through a CUSO or state league, staffed by two retired fraud investigators and a social worker. Record prevented losses and hold-to-report cycle time.

title: Beaver Warranty for County Culverts and Roads
one_liner: A 5-year no-clog guarantee that keeps beavers out of culverts using flow devices and sensors, and later sells the wetlands they build to water and wildfire agencies.
customer: County and municipal public works departments, state DOTs and railroads, and later water utilities and wildfire agencies.
problem: Beavers plug culverts, flooding roads and forcing repeated trapping, dam breaching and clearing, which costs taxpayers every year and never ends because new beavers arrive. Managers have no reliable, maintenance-free alternative and little data on true costs.
solution: A fixed-price warranty that installs proven flow devices (culvert fences and pond levelers), adds low-cost water-level sensors and cameras, and covers every follow-up visit. Evidence in hand: Virginia's DOT spent more than $300,000 a year on prevention, repairs and removal before devices, versus under $45,000 for installation and $277 a year to maintain; and Billerica, MA found trapping and breaching cost $409 per site per year versus $229 for devices. Well-designed culvert fences reportedly succeed 95% of the time. Once the culvert is solved, we offer beaver dam analogs and habitat as water storage and fire refuge.
why_now: California's Beaver Restoration Program (2023) had received 26 proposals by April 2026, and CDFW grants have funded over 100 beaver dam analogs. Wildfire and drought budgets are looking for nature-based solutions. Cheap IoT level sensors make a guarantee affordable to price and monitor.
revenue_model: Installs of roughly $8-45k per site or bundle, an annual monitoring and warranty fee of $300-1,000, and later performance contracts with water and fire agencies for stored water or refuge acres.
non_obvious_insight: The county does not pay to deal with beavers, it pays for recurring emergency labor, so sell an insurance-style warranty backed by data, not a wildlife product. After the culvert is fixed, the beaver becomes a free crew building water storage that a different agency will pay for, so the same animal is a liability line item for one customer and an asset for another.
first_30_days: File public-records requests in five counties for trapping and culvert-clearing spend. Offer to fix the three worst culverts at cost in exchange for cost data and a case study, then sell sub-$50k warranties that fit under small-purchase thresholds.
